The world's plants together produce about 140 million cubic metres of brine a day, most of it in the Gulf, a shallow, warm, nearly enclosed sea whose salinity has risen measurably since the plants were built along its shore. In an open coast with strong currents the brine is a manageable problem. In a gulf, a bay or a lagoon it is the plant's largest environmental cost, and the more plants a coast carries, the larger it grows.

Distance

The sea is at sea level. The people short of water are, more often than not, far from it and above it. Mexico City is at 2,200 metres and 300 kilometres from the coast. Tehran is at 1,200 metres and the nearest sea is the Caspian, over a mountain range. The North China Plain, the Punjab, the High Plains, the Sahel, the Central Valley: none is a coast. Lifting a cubic metre of water a thousand metres takes about three kilowatt hours, roughly what it took to desalinate it, and pumping it hundreds of kilometres takes more, so that the delivered cost doubles or triples before the water reaches the tap. The copper mines of the Atacama, described in their own article, do exactly this, lifting seawater three thousand metres to the mines, and they can because a tonne of copper is worth eight thousand dollars. A tonne of wheat is not.

Where it is going

The honest forecast for the industry, since I am in it, is growth. Capacity has doubled roughly every decade and will probably do so again, as membranes improve, as solar power makes the electricity cheap in the sunny places where the plants are, and as the coastal cities of India, China, Africa and the Americas reach the point that Chennai and Cape Town reached and decide they need a supply the rain does not control. The Gulf will keep building, the Mediterranean will build more, and the newest plants will be larger than any that exist. That growth will take the sea's share of the world's water from under one percent to perhaps two, over twenty years, in the cities that can pay. It will not reach the farms, and it will not reach inland, and every plant built will need an outfall, a power line and a tariff. The forecast is for a larger tool, used in the same kind of place, and the sentence at the top of this article will be as wrong in 2045 as it is now.

What the sentence leaves out

The sentence is comforting because it makes the problem technical, and technical problems have vendors. The places on this site that solved their water did not, for the most part, solve it with the sea. Singapore desalinates, and it also catches its rain, recycles its sewage and fixes its leaks. Israel desalinates, and it also drips its crops, reuses its wastewater and prices its water. Las Vegas has no desalination plant and has cut its river use by a quarter while growing by half. Orange County drinks its own sewage. Tokyo found a city's worth of water in its pipes. Every one of those is cheaper per cubic metre than the sea, and every one is available inland. The myth's harm lies in what it excuses: it lets a city, or a country, put off the cheaper and harder things, on the promise of a plant.

What the sea can and cannot do
Supply a coastal city that can pay a dollar a cubic metreYes, and it does
Replace a river or an aquifer for a city inland and uphillAt several times the cost, rarely
Supply irrigation for staple cropsNo, at any foreseeable price
Reduce the water a city needsNo; that is pricing, leaks and reuse
Make water without energy or brineNo; the floor is physics

The version that is true

There is a sentence about desalination that is right, and it is worth setting down beside the wrong one. For a coastal city that has done the cheaper things first, that has fixed its leaks, priced its water, reused its sewage and caught its rain, and that still needs a supply that does not depend on the sky, the sea is the next source, and it is now affordable, reliable and clean. Every city in this series that built a plant on those terms, Perth, Singapore, Israel's coast, has been glad of it. The cities that built one instead of the cheaper things, or that promised one and put off the rest, are the ones that will build a second plant and a third and still be short, because the demand a plant is built to meet is the demand the city never reduced. The sea is a good last answer. It is a poor first one.

What it teaches

Desalination is real, it works, and it is the right answer for a growing number of coastal cities, which is why my industry keeps building it. It is also under one percent of the world's water and cannot become much more, because most of the world's water is on farms that cannot pay for it and are nowhere near the sea. The world's water problem is, as every article on this site has said in its own way, a problem of how much is spent and where, and a plant on the coast changes neither. The sea is the answer to a particular question, asked by a particular kind of city. It is not the answer to the question.

One percent, at full capacity, from a sea that holds ninety seven.

Sources

  1. International Desalination Association and Global Water Intelligence, DesalData: global installed capacity of about 100 million cubic metres a day across some 20,000 plants.
  2. Jones, E. et al. (2019). The state of desalination and brine production: a global outlook. Science of the Total Environment 657. Brine volumes of about 1.5 litres per litre of product.
  3. FAO AQUASTAT: global freshwater withdrawals of about 4,000 cubic kilometres a year, about 70 percent for agriculture.
  4. Voutchkov, N. (2018). Energy use for membrane seawater desalination: current status and trends. Desalination 431. About 3 to 4 kilowatt hours per cubic metre.
  5. Israel Water Authority, share of domestic supply from desalination, and Sorek and Hadera plant costs of around 0.5 dollars per cubic metre.
  6. Photographs: opener: 160810-N-FP878-007 (28801419432) by Commander, U.S. Naval Forces Europe-Afri (public domain) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Wheat farm located along Clark Rd in Pasco by Araceli Fuentes (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Reuven Rivlin in a visit at IDE - Sorek Desalination Plant (0097) by Mark Neyman (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Myth: Boiling water removes everything
item.description:
"If in doubt, boil it." Good advice, and it covers half of what can be wrong with water.
Boiling kills. One minute at a rolling boil, three at altitude, and every bacterium, virus and parasite in the water is dead, including the Cryptosporidium that chlorine cannot touch. That is why a boil water notice is the right response to a burst main or a failed filter, and why boiling has saved more lives than any other water treatment in history.
Boiling does not remove anything. Salt, nitrate, lead, arsenic, pesticides, the fluoride in the tap and the dissolved solids that make the kettle fur: all of it stays in the pan, and since some of the water leaves as steam, what remains is slightly more concentrated than before. The scale in the kettle is the proof. It is the dissolved minerals, made visible by the heat, and none of them went anywhere.
Two problems, two tools. Microbes: boil. Chemistry: a filter, a membrane, or a different source. The kettle only ever solved the first.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
A rolling boil is the oldest water treatment there is, and it does one job perfectly: it kills. What boiling does to the microbes, what it leaves untouched, what it makes slightly worse, and why a boil water notice and a lead pipe warning are asking for two different things.

When a water main bursts and the utility issues a boil water notice, it is relying on the oldest treatment there is. Boiling has been used to make water safe since before anyone knew what was in it, and it has probably saved more lives than every chlorination plant put together. It is also the source of a belief that goes well beyond what the kettle can do: that boiled water is clean water, full stop. This article separates the two claims, because one of them is true and the other, in the situations where it matters most, is the opposite of true.

The claim

Boiling water removes everything. Stated as a household rule, and applied, in practice, to any water that seems doubtful: cloudy water, water after a flood, water in a country with an unfamiliar tap, water from an old pipe.

What boiling does perfectly

Boiling kills. Bacteria, viruses and the protozoa that cause waterborne disease are living things with proteins that unfold at temperatures well below the boiling point, and a rolling boil finishes the job on all of them. Cholera, typhoid, the E. coli of a contaminated well, hepatitis A, norovirus, Giardia and, importantly, Cryptosporidium, the parasite whose tough cyst shrugs off chlorine and made 400,000 people ill in Milwaukee in 1993, as the disinfection article recounts: all of them die in a pan.

Boiling water for safety
At sea levelBring to a rolling boil and hold for one minute
Above about 2,000 metres, where water boils coolerHold for three minutes
Cloudy waterLet it settle or strain it through cloth first, then boil
AfterwardsCool covered, store in a clean container, use within a day

This is why a boil water notice is the right response to a burst main, a failed filter or a flood, all of which can let microbes into a supply that is otherwise safe. It is why travellers are told to boil, and why the advice has held for a century in every language. Against the biology of water, the kettle is as good as a treatment plant.

What boiling leaves untouched

Boiling removes nothing. That is the half of the rule that fails, and it fails in the situations where people most often reach for the kettle.

Everything that is dissolved in water stays dissolved when the water boils, because boiling only changes the water. Salt stays. Nitrate from fertiliser stays. Fluoride stays. The metals that come from pipes and from the ground, lead, copper, arsenic, stay. Pesticides and industrial chemicals stay, apart from the few that are volatile enough to leave with the steam. The dissolved solids described in the article on TDS stay, all of them, which is the point of that article: nothing catches a dissolved substance except a membrane, a resin or distillation, and a saucepan is none of those.

What boiling does and does not do
Bacteria, viruses, parasitesKilled
Salt and dissolved mineralsUntouched, and concentrated
NitrateUntouched, and concentrated
Lead, copper, arsenic and other metalsUntouched, and concentrated
Pesticides and most industrial chemicalsMostly untouched
ChlorineDriven off, which removes the taste and the protection
Cloudiness from particlesNot removed, unless the water settles

What boiling makes slightly worse

Worse than untouched, in fact, because some of the water leaves. A pan at a rolling boil loses water as steam, and what stays behind holds all of the dissolved substances in less water. Boil a litre down to nine tenths and every dissolved concentration has risen by a tenth. It is a small effect, and it is in the wrong direction, and for water that is doubtful because of its chemistry rather than its biology, boiling makes it marginally worse while creating a feeling of safety that is entirely false.

The kettle proves it. The scale that builds on the element is calcium and magnesium that were dissolved in the water and came out of solution when it was heated, as the hard water article explains. They were in the water before, invisible. Boiling did not remove them; it made them visible, in the kettle, and left the rest in the cup. A person who boils hard water to purify it is looking at the evidence that it does not work every time they descale.

Two notices, two problems

The clearest way to see the difference is in the two warnings a water utility issues, which sound alike and ask for opposite things.

A boil water notice follows a microbial risk: a burst main that let groundwater in, a positive test for E. coli, a failure at the disinfection stage, a flood. It says: the biology of your water may be unsafe, boil it, and the advice is complete. Boiling fixes the problem entirely.

A do not drink notice, or a lead warning of the kind that Flint's residents should have received in 2014, as the pH article recounts, follows a chemical risk: lead from pipes, a chemical spill upstream, nitrate above the limit, arsenic in a well. It says: the chemistry of your water is unsafe, and boiling will not help. The water needs a filter certified for the substance, a different source, or bottled water until the cause is fixed. Boiling lead contaminated water, as the American environmental agency's guidance says plainly, does not remove the lead and can increase its concentration.

NoticeThe problemThe fix
Boil waterMicrobes: burst main, failed disinfection, floodBoil for one minute
Do not drinkChemistry: lead, nitrate, arsenic, a spillA certified filter, another source, or bottled water

Distillation, which is not boiling

There is a way to make boiling remove things, and it is the one people are half remembering when they trust the kettle. If the steam is caught and condensed, the water that results is distilled, and it has left everything dissolved behind in the pot. Distillation is how the first desalination plants made fresh water from the sea, as the desalination article recounts, and it is what a solar still does: a dark tray of dirty water under a sloping sheet of glass, with the sun evaporating the water and the glass condensing it into a channel. A survival still of that kind makes a litre or two a day, and the water is pure enough to be flat and tasteless, because the minerals that give water its taste were left behind with the salt. The kettle boils but does not condense, and that is the whole difference. The steam that carries pure water away is the steam that fogs the kitchen window.

Filters, and what each one removes

For the chemistry that boiling cannot touch, the household tools are filters, and they are not all the same.

A jug filter with activated carbon removes chlorine, which improves the taste, and some organic compounds, and it reduces lead and copper if the cartridge is designed to and is changed on time. It removes no nitrate, no salt and no fluoride. An under sink reverse osmosis unit, a small version of the membrane described in its own article, removes nearly everything dissolved, including nitrate, salt, fluoride and metals, and produces a stream of concentrate to the drain as its larger cousins do. A ceramic or hollow fibre filter removes microbes without chemicals, and is the traveller's alternative to boiling. None of them is a kettle, and the kettle is none of them. The cheapest way to know which is needed is the utility's published results for the tap, which say what is in the water before anyone decides how to treat it.

Why the belief is so strong

The rule survives because it was once the whole truth. For most of human history the dangers in water were living, and the kettle answered them. Cholera, typhoid and dysentery killed more people than any chemical in a pipe, and the advice to boil was the difference between an outbreak and a quiet summer, in every army camp, every city slum and every colonial household with a servant and a stove. The chemical problems of water, lead, nitrate, arsenic, industrial solvents, arrived later, with the industries that made them, and they arrived in cities whose biology had already been fixed by the treatment plant. The belief is a survivor from the age before the plant, and it is right about that age. It is only in the age after, when the tap is safe from microbes and the remaining risks are dissolved, that the kettle's reputation exceeds its powers.

The nuance

The rule holds, entirely, for the problem it was made for. Where water is doubtful because of what might be living in it, which is the case in most of the world and in most emergencies, boiling is the best available treatment, and the advice to boil is the advice that saves lives. Nothing in this article should make anyone hesitate to boil water they suspect.

It fails for the problem that a modern city's water is more likely to have. In a city with a working treatment plant and a chlorine residual, the microbes are handled, and the risks that remain are old pipes, industrial chemistry and the ground the water came through, none of which the kettle touches. In that setting, boiling tap water for safety achieves nothing except driving off the chlorine that was protecting it, and a person worried about lead from their own plumbing is better served by running the tap for a minute in the morning and fitting a filter than by boiling anything.

Two problems, two tools

Water can be unsafe in two ways, and the ways need different tools. Living things are killed by heat, and the kettle kills them all. Dissolved things are removed only by a membrane, a resin, or distillation, and the kettle removes none of them. The oldest water treatment in the world does its one job perfectly and has been asked, for centuries, to do a second one that it cannot. The scale on the element has been trying to say so all along.

Sources

  1. World Health Organization, Guidelines for Drinking water Quality, and WHO technical brief on boiling water: a rolling boil is sufficient to inactivate pathogenic bacteria, viruses and protozoa.
  2. US Centers for Disease Control, guidance on boil water advisories: one minute at a rolling boil, three minutes above 2,000 metres.
  3. US EPA, guidance on lead in drinking water: boiling does not remove lead and may increase its concentration.
  4. Photographs: opener: Person pours water from yellow kettle in wooden kitchen by Shixart1985 (CC BY) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: 2008-07-05 Water boiling in cooking pot by Ildar Sagdejev (Specious) (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Billycan-campfire (cropped) by Flickr user "Johan Larsson" (CC BY) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Myth: A bath uses more water than a shower
item.description:
"A shower uses less water than a bath." It depends, and the modern shower has quietly overturned the rule.
A full standard bath holds about 80 litres, and a large one 150. A typical shower head delivers 8 to 10 litres a minute, so a five minute shower is 40 to 50 litres and a bath wins by nothing. A power shower delivers 15 litres a minute or more, and ten minutes under one is 150 litres, a large bath. The average shower in Britain lasts seven to eight minutes, which puts it, at a typical head, level with a bath.
The line is easy to find. Time the shower, put a bucket under the head for a minute to measure the flow, and multiply. Under 80 litres and the shower wins. Over it and the bath was the economical choice all along.
The water is the smaller half of it. Heating that water is the largest energy use in most homes after the heating itself, and every litre of hot water, bath or shower, was heated by gas or electricity.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
Everyone knows a shower saves water. The numbers say it depends on the shower head, the minutes and the size of the bath, and that the modern power shower has quietly overturned the rule. What a bath and a shower actually use, how to know which side of the line you are on, and why the water is the smaller half of the story.

Of all the water advice that everyone has absorbed without checking, the rule that a shower uses less water than a bath is the most confidently repeated. It was true when it was coined, in an age of trickling electric showers and deep enamel baths, and it is the reason a generation of people feel virtuous under the shower and guilty in the tub. The numbers have moved since. This article measures both, finds where the line falls, and then points out that the water was never the larger half of the question.

The claim

A shower uses less water than a bath. Stated as a rule, without conditions, and usually followed by a suggestion that a bath is an indulgence.

What a bath holds

A standard bath, the kind fitted in most European homes, holds about 80 litres when filled to a normal bathing depth, and up to about 120 if filled to the overflow. A large or deep bath holds 150 or more. A shallow bath, run for a child, might be 40. The volume is fixed by the bath and the depth, and it does not change with how long the person stays in it, which is the bath's quiet advantage.

BathLitres
Shallow, for a childAbout 40
Standard, filled to bathing depthAbout 80
Standard, filled to the overflowAbout 120
Large or deep bath150 or more

What a shower uses

A shower's water is its flow rate multiplied by its minutes, and both vary more than most people realise.

An old style electric shower, heating water as it passes through a small element, delivers 4 to 6 litres a minute, which is the trickle the rule was built on. A modern mixer shower, fed from a hot water cylinder or a combination boiler, delivers 8 to 10. A power shower, with a pump, delivers 13 to 16 or more, and the large rainfall heads sold for luxury bathrooms can pass 20. The minutes are the other half: surveys in Britain put the average shower at about seven and a half minutes, and teenagers, as every parent knows, at considerably more.

ShowerLitres a minuteFive minutesEight minutesTwelve minutes
Electric showerAbout 5254060
Mixer shower8 to 1040 to 5065 to 8095 to 120
Power shower13 to 1665 to 80105 to 130155 to 190
Large rainfall headUp to 20100160240

Where the line falls

Put the two tables together and the rule dissolves.

A five minute shower under any head uses less than a standard bath. An eight minute shower under a mixer, which is the average British shower under the commonest kind of head, uses about 80 litres, which is the bath. An eight minute power shower uses more than the bath, and a twelve minute one under a rainfall head uses three baths. The shower wins clearly only when it is short, or the head is modest, and it loses clearly when it is long and the head is generous, which describes a great many modern bathrooms.

The verdict
Short shower, any headThe shower wins
Average shower, mixer headLevel with a bath
Average shower, power showerThe bath wins
Long shower, any modern headThe bath wins, sometimes by a lot

The verdict, then, is that it depends, and that the modern shower has quietly overturned a rule that was written for a different appliance. A person who takes long showers under a power shower and feels virtuous about skipping baths has the sums the wrong way round.

How to know which side you are on

The line is easy to find at home, with a bucket and a watch.

Put a bucket under the shower head, run the shower as you normally would, and time how long it takes to collect ten litres; a bucket usually has a mark. Divide, and that is the flow rate in litres a minute. Then time an ordinary shower, from turning on to turning off. Multiply the two, and compare with 80. Under it, the shower is the economical choice. Over it, the bath was, all along, and the cheaper fix is a shorter shower or a lower flow head rather than a change of habit.

Low flow shower heads, which mix air into the water to keep the feel of a full spray at 6 to 8 litres a minute, are the single most effective change, and they cost a few tens of euros. A shower timer, of the kind Cape Town's households used in 2018 as the Day Zero article describes, is the second. The city that cut its water use in half did it largely by cutting its showers to two minutes, which is 20 litres under any head.

The larger half of the story

Water is the smaller half of a bath or a shower, and it is worth saying so in an article about water.

Every litre of hot water in a home was heated, by gas, oil or electricity, from the temperature of the mains to about forty degrees, and heating water is the largest use of energy in most homes after heating the rooms, somewhere around a sixth of the household's total. A litre of hot water costs far more in energy than in water, and it carries a carbon cost that the water itself does not. So the question of bath against shower, honestly asked, is about hot litres, and the answer is the same as before: fewer minutes and a lower flow head save more than any choice between the two fixtures.

There is also the water's journey, which the rest of this series describes. Every litre that went down the bath or shower drain is greywater, lightly used and warm, and in a house with the plumbing for it, described in the greywater article, it would have flushed the toilet before it left.

The rest of the bathroom

The bath and the shower are the largest uses of water in a home, and they are not the only ones, and the rest of the room is worth measuring while the bucket is out.

The toilet is the second largest, at around a quarter of household water. An old cistern uses 9 to 13 litres a flush; a modern dual flush uses 4 to 6, and swapping one for the other saves more than most changes to showering. A running tap delivers about 6 litres a minute, so brushing teeth with the tap open for two minutes uses 12, which is a short shower's worth every morning and evening. A washing machine uses around 50 litres a cycle, a dishwasher around 10 to 15, and both use less than the same job done by hand under a running tap. A dripping tap loses several litres a day, and a leaking cistern, which is common and silent, can lose hundreds.

The rest of the home, per useLitres
Old toilet cistern, per flush9 to 13
Modern dual flush, per flush4 to 6
Tap running, per minuteAbout 6
Washing machine, per cycleAbout 50
Dishwasher, per cycle10 to 15
A person in Britain, per day, all usesAbout 140

A person in Britain uses about 140 litres a day at home, of which the bathroom is well over half. Cape Town's households, in 2018, lived on 50. The gap between the two numbers is almost entirely the shower and the toilet, and the bucket, the timer and the dual flush cistern are the whole of the difference.

The bath's other trick

A bath has one more property that the rule never mentions: its water is still there when the bather gets out. Eighty litres of warm, lightly soapy greywater sits in the tub, and in a house with a garden, a bucket and a little patience, it waters the beds, rinses the paths or, as Cape Town's households found in 2018, flushes the toilet for the rest of the day. A shower's water is gone down the drain the moment it has done its work. Neither fact changes the arithmetic of the rule, but a bath that is used twice is, on the day, the more economical of the two by a wide margin, and in a drought it is the one the water industry quietly recommends.

Where the rule came from

The rule dates from the 1970s and 1980s, when the electric shower arrived in British and European bathrooms as a cheap alternative to a hot water cylinder, and it was true of that appliance: a small element could heat only a trickle, four or five litres a minute, and a five minute wash under it used a quarter of a bath. The water companies and the energy campaigns of the period repeated it, reasonably, and it entered the culture. The mixer shower, the combination boiler and then the pumped power shower followed over the next thirty years, each delivering more water than the last, and the rule was never revised. It is a good example of advice that was measured once, for one appliance, and repeated for forty years about a different one.

The nuance

The rule holds in some cases. It is right for the appliance it was written for: a short shower under a modest head against a full bath. It was right for most bathrooms in 1980. It is wrong for a great many bathrooms in 2026, and it is wrong in a way that flatters the person breaking it.

A bath is a fixed 80 litres, decided by the bath. A shower is a variable, decided by the head and the person, and it can be 20 litres or 250. That is the whole finding. The bath does not deserve its reputation, and the shower does not deserve its halo; the number is in the minutes, and the bucket will tell you what yours is.

Sources

  1. Waterwise (UK) and the Energy Saving Trust, At Home with Water (2013): bath volumes, shower flow rates, average shower duration of about seven and a half minutes, and hot water as a share of household energy.
  2. Energy Saving Trust: typical mixer shower 8 to 10 litres a minute; power showers 13 to 16 litres a minute or more; a standard bath about 80 litres.
  3. European Commission ecodesign and water label data: flow rates of shower heads and taps.
  4. Photographs: opener: High speed shower filtered by turydddu @ Flickr, retouched by JovanCormac (CC BY) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Bathtub of Khan Pool Suite in Amantaka luxury Resort & Hotel in Luang Prabang Laos by Basile Morin (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Itron Water Meter by Ganesh Dhamodkar (CC BY) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Thirsty: Wine
item.description:
Almost every farmer on Earth is trying to get more water to their crop. Winemakers are the strange exception. They spend their careers trying to make the plant a little thirsty.
A vine with plenty of water grows big, watery grapes and lots of leaves. A vine that has to work sends its roots down and produces small grapes with concentrated flavour, which is what ends up tasting like something. Growers call the technique deficit irrigation, and in parts of Europe the rules go further: several famous appellations simply forbid irrigation, on the grounds that a vineyard that needs watering is planted in the wrong place.
All of which makes the number a little awkward. A glass of wine still carries about 109 litres of water, and per litre wine costs roughly three times what beer does. Grapes are not especially thirsty; there just are not many of them per bottle, and the vine drinks rain all season either way.
The part worth watching is what heat is doing to those old rules. Regions that built their identity on never irrigating are facing summers their vines were not planted for, and some of the bans have quietly started to bend.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
Almost every farmer on Earth is trying to get more water to their crop. Winemakers are the exception, spending their careers keeping the vine a little thirsty. A glass of wine still carries about 109 litres, three times what beer does per litre, and the old rules about not watering vines are starting to bend in the heat.

Walk through a vineyard in August in the south of France and the ground between the rows is bare and cracked, the leaves are small, and the vines look, to anyone used to a garden, as if somebody has forgotten to water them. Nobody has forgotten. In most of the famous wine regions of Europe the vines are not watered on purpose, and for a long time it was against the rules to water them at all. Wine is the one crop on this site whose growers spend their careers keeping the plant slightly thirsty, and that makes its water footprint an odd one to read.

A hundred and nine litres

By the Water Footprint Network's method, wine comes to about 869 litres of water per litre in the global average, counting the rain the vines took up, the irrigation applied where there was any, and the clean water it would take to dilute the pollution from the vineyard and the winery. A 125 millilitre glass is a seventh of that, about 109 litres.

StageLitresShare
Growing the grapes10092%
Winery cleaning65%
The bottle and the rest33%

The split is approximate; the total is the citable figure. As with everything on this site that grows, the vineyard is nearly all of it, and the winery, where the water goes on washing tanks, barrels and floors, is a small share.

Per litre, wine costs roughly three times what beer does, at 869 litres against 298. Grapes are not especially thirsty as fruit go, at around 600 litres per kilogram, well below an avocado. The difference is concentration: it takes somewhere between 1.2 and 1.5 kilograms of grapes to make a bottle of wine, where a litre of beer needs less than 200 grams of grain, and the water follows the fruit.

The vine wanted less

Here is the fact that sets wine apart from every other footprint in the series. A vine with plenty of water grows a big canopy of leaves and large, watery grapes, and the wine made from them is thin. A vine that has to work for its water sends its roots deep, sets fewer and smaller grapes, and concentrates sugar, acid and flavour into them, and that is the wine that ends up tasting like something. The plant, mildly stressed, makes a better product.

Growers have known this for centuries, and the modern name for managing it deliberately is deficit irrigation: giving the vine less water than it would take if offered, at the stages of the season when a little stress improves the fruit, and enough at the stages when it would only do harm. In the New World, in California, Australia, Chile and Argentina, most vineyards are irrigated and the deficit is managed with a valve. In much of Europe the deficit is managed by planting the vine in a place where the rain is a little short, and leaving it to cope.

What water does to a vine
Plenty of waterLarge canopy, big watery grapes, thin wine
A managed shortageDeep roots, small concentrated grapes, better wine
Too littleStalled ripening, lost crop

That is why the vineyard in August looks neglected. The bare ground and the small leaves are the point.

The rule that forbade watering

In the appellation system that governs the classic wine regions of France, and in the similar systems of Italy and Spain, the vine's thirst was written into law. For most of the twentieth century French rules prohibited irrigating vines during the growing season in appellation vineyards, on the principle that a vineyard which needed watering was planted in the wrong place, and that the character of a wine came from the land and the weather it was given rather than from a pipe. Several of the most famous appellations kept, and still keep, outright bans.

The result is a wine footprint that, in Europe, is almost entirely green. The vine drinks what falls on it, over a season, from the soil, and the 869 litres per litre in the global average is mostly rain on a hillside that was going to be rained on regardless. Irrigated New World vineyards carry a blue share, drawn from rivers in dry valleys, and it is worth knowing which bottle came from where.

Where the world's wine grows, and on what

The global average hides two different industries. The old wine countries of Europe, France, Italy and Spain, still make around half the world's wine, mostly in temperate or Mediterranean climates where winter rain stores enough moisture in the soil to carry an unirrigated vine through summer, and where the rules described above kept the pipes out. Their footprint is green almost to the last litre.

The newer wine regions were planted where the sun was reliable and the rain was not. The vineyards of Australia's Murray Darling basin, of California's Central Valley, of Chile's central valleys and of Argentina's Mendoza, a desert at the foot of the Andes, produce wine of every quality, and nearly all of it on irrigation drawn from rivers and aquifers that other users, cities and other crops among them, also depend on. In a drought year the competition is direct. During Australia's long drought of the 2000s the price of water rights in the Murray Darling basin rose until some growers found it paid better to sell their water than to make wine with it, and the vineyards that survived were the ones with the deepest pockets or the oldest rights.

Where wine growsWhat the vines drink
The classic European regionsWinter rain stored in the soil, and the rules forbid much else
Australia, California, Chile, Argentina, South AfricaIrrigation from rivers and aquifers, managed by deficit
Cooler new regions, New Zealand, Oregon, EnglandMostly rain

A bottle from Bordeaux and a bottle from Mendoza can carry a similar number of litres, and in one case they fell from the sky onto a field that would have been rained on anyway, and in the other they were pumped from a river in a desert. As with every product on this site, the label's most useful line, for water, is the one that says where.

Grapes per bottle

The arithmetic that makes wine three times beer is worth a moment, because it is not about the plant being thirsty. A vine uses water roughly the way any fruit tree does, and grapes at around 600 litres per kilogram are middling among fruits. The multiplier is yield. A bottle of wine needs between 1.2 and 1.5 kilograms of grapes, crushed and pressed, and the skins, seeds and stems, a quarter of the weight, are left behind as pomace. A litre of beer needs under 200 grams of barley. Wine simply contains more crop per glass, and the deficit irrigation that makes it taste of something lowers the yield further, concentrating the water along with the flavour.

The winery

The winery's water is a small share and a familiar story. Grapes are crushed, the juice or the must is fermented in tanks, the wine is racked from vessel to vessel, aged, filtered and bottled, and every tank, hose, press and barrel is washed between uses, because grape sugar feeds every microbe that would spoil a wine as readily as the yeast that makes it. A winery uses somewhere between two and six litres of water for every litre of wine, nearly all of it cleaning, and the water that leaves carries sugar, yeast and lees, and is treated like a brewery's or a dairy's, increasingly by digestion into biogas. Harvest is the pressure point: a winery may crush its whole year's fruit in six weeks, and its water use and its effluent peak with it.

The rule is starting to bend

The part of the story worth watching is what heat is doing to the old rules. Regions that built their identity on never irrigating are facing summers their vines were not planted for: longer droughts, higher temperatures, ripening that races ahead of flavour, and in the worst years vines that simply stop. France permitted irrigation under conditions in 2006 and has extended the derogations in drought years since. Individual appellations have loosened their own rules through the 2010s and 2020s, allowing drip lines to be laid in vineyards where a decade earlier they would have cost a grower the right to use the name on the label. Southern Spain and parts of Italy have moved the same way.

A tradition built around scarcity is running into actual scarcity, and the argument inside the wine world is a real one. Irrigation keeps a vineyard alive in a summer it would not otherwise survive. It also risks producing exactly the large, watery grapes the tradition was designed to avoid, and it draws on rivers and aquifers in regions that are drying for the same reason the vines are struggling. The likely outcome is a middle: deficit irrigation, managed by hand and by sensor, in places that used to manage it by faith.

Reading the number

A glass of wine at 109 litres is a large number for a small glass, and it is mostly rain on a hillside, drunk by a plant that its growers were trying to keep slightly short. Of all the footprints in this series it is the one where more water would make a worse product, which is a useful thing to keep in mind about numbers. The interesting question about wine is the one the vineyards are answering now, summer by summer: how long a crop that was built on thirst can go on doing without.

Sources

  1. Mekonnen, M.M. and Hoekstra, A.Y. (2011). The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 15. Wine about 869 L/L, grapes about 608 L/kg, beer about 298 L/L, global averages.
  2. Stage split (grapes, winery cleaning, bottle and the rest) is approximate and illustrative; the total is the citable figure.
  3. Chaves, M.M. et al. (2010). Grapevine under deficit irrigation: hints from physiological and molecular data. Annals of Botany 105. The physiology of deficit irrigation and fruit quality.
  4. French appellation rules on irrigation (INAO): historically prohibited during the growing season, permitted since 2006 under conditions and by derogation in drought years, with several appellations relaxing their own rules through the 2010s and 2020s.
  5. Winery water use of roughly 2 to 6 litres per litre of wine, from published winery benchmarks.
  6. Photographs: opener: Opus One Glass, Wine, & Vineyard (to be trimmed) by Dave Minogue (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Malbec grapes on the vine by Micah MacAllen (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Winery receiving grapes during harvest by David Burn (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Thirsty: Avocado
item.description:
This series has spent a lot of posts arguing that a big water number is not automatically bad news. Chocolate drinks tropical rain. Coffee mostly does too. The avocado is where that argument stops.
The difference is where the water comes from. Cocoa trees stand in some of the wettest places on Earth and drink what falls on them. Avocados prefer dry Mediterranean climates, which means Chile, Spain, Mexico, California, and in those places the water arrives through a pipe. Someone pumped it out of a river or a well, and it was not available for anything else afterwards.
Petorca in Chile is the case everyone in the water world knows. A fruit growing province where plantations expanded fast, rivers ran low, and residents ended up receiving drinking water by tanker truck while orchards nearby stayed green. That is a truck in a village rather than a footprint calculation.
None of which makes avocados forbidden. It makes them the fruit where origin actually matters, and the sticker on the skin says more about water than any number on a chart.
The long version, with the fruit table and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
Every footprint on this site has argued that a big water number is not automatically bad news. The avocado is where that argument stops. About 400 litres for one fruit, and in the dry places where avocados grow, that water arrives through a pipe, from a river or a well that had other uses for it.

Most of the footprints on this site come with a reassurance attached. Coffee carries 140 litres, and nearly all of it was rain on a hillside that was going to be rained on anyway. Chocolate carries 1,700, and 98 percent of it fell on a farm in the wet tropics. Beef, bread and milk are mostly rain on fields and pasture. The numbers are large, and the article goes on to explain why they are less alarming than they look.

The avocado is where that argument stops. Its number is not the largest on this site, and it is not the smallest. What sets it apart is the kind of water it is, and where.

Four hundred litres

By the Water Footprint Network's method, avocados come to about 2,000 litres of water per kilogram in the global average. An avocado of 200 grams is therefore about 400 litres, and a smaller fruit of 160 grams, which is the assumption behind the 320 litre figure often quoted, a little less. Both numbers come from the same research and differ only in the size of the fruit.

FruitLitres per kilogram
Avocadoabout 2,000
Mangoabout 1,800
Appleabout 820
Bananaabout 790

Per kilogram, an avocado sits at the top of the fruit table, above the mango and more than twice the apple. That is a matter of botany: the avocado is an oily fruit from a large evergreen tree that yields modestly, and the litres per kilogram follow, as they do for every tree crop. It is not, on its own, a reason for concern. The reason for concern is in the next section.

Pumped, not rained

Cocoa and coffee are crops of the wet tropics, and their footprints are green because rain is what they grow on. The avocado is a crop of the dry Mediterranean climate: hot summers, mild winters, and long months with no rain at all. The world's avocados come from Mexico above all, then from Chile, Peru, Spain, Israel, South Africa, Kenya, California and Australia, and in nearly every one of those places the growing season is the dry season and the water arrives through a pipe.

An avocado orchard in summer is irrigated, from a river, a canal or a well, for months on end. That water was pumped by someone, it was not going to fall on the orchard by itself, and once it has passed through the trees it is not available to anyone else. In the footprint that shows up as a large blue share, and blue water is the kind that a river is missing afterwards.

CropWhere it growsWhat it grows on
CocoaThe wet tropicsRain, almost entirely
CoffeeTropical highlandsMostly rain
AvocadoDry Mediterranean climatesIrrigation, in the dry season

This is the whole difference between the avocado and the reassuring footprints that came before it. The number is similar. The water is a different kind, from a different place, with other people waiting for it.

Petorca

Everyone who works in water knows the name of one Chilean province, because it is the case where the footprint stopped being a calculation and became a truck.

Petorca, north of Santiago, is a dry valley that became one of Chile's largest avocado growing regions from the 1990s onwards, as plantations spread up the hillsides on the strength of export demand. The valley's rivers, never large, were drawn down by the orchards' wells and the water rights that Chile's system allowed to be bought and traded. By the 2010s the rivers ran dry for long stretches, the shallow wells that villages depended on failed, and residents of the valley were receiving their drinking water by tanker truck, a few dozen litres per person per day, while the orchards on the slopes above them stayed green. Investigations by Danish and British journalists in 2017 and 2018 put the province on front pages in the countries that bought the fruit, and Petorca has been the reference case for avocados and water ever since.

None of this is captured by a footprint number. Four hundred litres for a fruit describes the water. It does not describe the well that failed, the truck in the village, or the fact that the water in the fruit and the water the village lacked were the same water. That is what blue water means when it is looked at closely, and Petorca is the clearest picture of it.

How the orchard is watered

An avocado tree is a large evergreen that keeps its leaves all year and transpires through all of them, and in the climates where it is grown commercially it needs something like a thousand millimetres of water a year, most of it in the months when none falls. The tree is shallow rooted and intolerant of both drought and waterlogging, so the water has to be delivered often and in measured amounts, which in a modern orchard means drip lines or micro sprinklers under every tree, fed from a pump.

The pump draws from wherever the grower has rights: a canal from a river, a borehole into the aquifer, a reservoir filled in winter. Drip irrigation is efficient, in the sense that little is wasted between the pipe and the root, and the industry is right to say so. Efficiency, though, changes how much is taken from the river, and not where the water came from. A drip irrigated orchard in a dry valley is a smaller draw on the river than a flooded one, and it is still a draw, in a season when the river has least to give.

Chile's water code

Petorca is also the story of a law. In 1981, under the Pinochet government, Chile adopted a water code that separated water rights from land and made them private property, to be bought, sold and held like any other asset. The idea was that a market would move water to its most valuable use. In a dry valley with a booming export crop, it did exactly that: the rights flowed to the orchards that could pay for them, and away from the small farmers and villages that could not. When the rivers fell, the holders of the rights were entitled to their water and the villages were entitled to a tanker.

The code was amended in 2022, after years of drought and protest, to declare water a public good for human consumption first and to limit new rights in stressed basins. The orchards remain, the old rights remain, and the reform is a beginning rather than a solution. But Petorca made the argument, in a way that no footprint number could, that the water in a fruit is also a question of who was allowed to take it.

The demand side

The reason the orchards spread is on the other end of the supply chain. Avocado consumption in Europe and North America has multiplied several times over in two decades, from a specialist fruit to a supermarket staple, and the growers of Chile, Peru, Mexico and Spain planted to meet it. Peru's avocados come largely from the Ica valley, a coastal desert where the aquifer has been drawn down by export agriculture in much the same way as Petorca's rivers. The market that made the fruit ordinary is a long way from the valleys that grow it, and it has, until recently, seen none of the cost.

Michoacán, and the others

Petorca is the famous case, and it is not the only one. Michoacán in Mexico, which grows more avocados than any other region on Earth, has seen forest cleared for orchards, wells drilled without permits, and disputes over water that have turned violent. In Spain's Málaga province, avocado growing in a region already short of water has become a political question in dry years. In each case the pattern is the same: a valuable export crop that needs water through the dry months, in a place that does not have water to spare, and a market a long way away that does not see what it costs.

Not every avocado comes from a place like this. Kenya and parts of Colombia grow avocados largely on rain; so do wetter parts of Mexico. The trouble is that the fruit on a shelf does not say, and the country of origin, which it does say, is the best guide a buyer has.

What the sticker says

None of this makes avocados forbidden, and a boycott would hurt the growers of Petorca before it helped anyone. What it makes them is the fruit where origin actually matters, more than for anything else on this site. The country on the sticker is a better guide to the water in an avocado than any number on a chart, because the number is much the same everywhere and the water behind it is not. A fruit from a rainy region and a fruit from a drought zone are, in water terms, different purchases, and this is the one product where a shopper can tell them apart at the shelf.

Reading the number

The avocado closes the first run of footprints on this site, and it closes an argument. The argument was that a large water number is a starting point rather than a verdict, that the colours of the water matter more than the total, and that most large numbers, looked at closely, turn out to be rain. All of that is still true. The avocado is the fruit that shows what the argument looks like when it fails: a modest number, a dry valley, and a truck.

Sources

  1. Mekonnen, M.M. and Hoekstra, A.Y. (2011). The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 15. Avocado about 1,981 L/kg, mango about 1,800, apple about 822, banana about 790, global averages.
  2. Reporting on the Petorca province, Chile: Danwatch (2017), Avocados and stolen water; subsequent coverage by the Guardian, Reuters and Chilean media on tanker truck deliveries and the province's water emergency.
  3. Chile, Código de Aguas (1981) and its reform, Law 21.435 (2022), on private water rights and the priority of human consumption.
  4. Both the 320 and 400 litre figures for one avocado derive from the same per kilogram footprint and differ only in the assumed weight of the fruit.
  5. Photographs: opener: Avocado Hass - single and halved by Ivar Leidus (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Avocado and lemon orchards, California (9323) by Lance Cheung/USDA (public domain) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Avocados from the orchard by MaiDenzel (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Plain Water: TDS
item.description:
Pick up a bottle of mineral water and look near the bottom of the label. There will be a line saying dry residue at 180 degrees, followed by a number. That number is TDS, total dissolved solids, and once you know it you will read water differently.
It is everything dissolved into the water: salt, calcium, magnesium, whatever the water met on its way through the ground. Rain has almost none. Tap water runs a few hundred milligrams per litre. Seawater sits around 35,000.
Two things follow. The first is that TDS is what water tastes like. Water with nothing in it tastes flat, which is why distilled water is unpleasant and why mineral water brands advertise their minerals instead of hiding them. The second is that dissolved is the hard problem in my industry. A filter catches things by being too small to let them through, and dissolved salt has come apart into pieces far smaller than any pore. You cannot strain it, settle it, or feed it to bacteria. The only ways out are a membrane at very high pressure, boiling, or a resin, and all three cost energy. That is why salt is the wall every water recycling project eventually hits.
The long version, with the scale, the measurement and the three ways out, is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water
item.content:encoded:
Total dissolved solids is the single most useful measurement in the water business. It explains why water tastes of anything, why limescale forms in a kettle, and why the hardest part of cleaning water is the part nobody can see.

Every bottle of mineral water sold in Europe carries, somewhere near the bottom of its label, a line of small print that almost nobody reads. It says something like dry residue at 180 °C, and it is followed by a number. Depending on the brand the number might be 50, or 300, or well over a thousand. The units are milligrams per litre.

That line is the closest most people ever come to the measurement that the water industry uses more than any other. It has an unlovely name, total dissolved solids, and a three letter abbreviation, TDS, that engineers say without thinking. Once it is understood, a surprising amount of everyday water makes sense: why one water tastes of something and another of nothing, why a kettle furs up, why a desalination plant costs what it does, and why the last step in cleaning water is always the most expensive.

What dissolved means

Water is a remarkable solvent. As it moves through soil and rock it takes things with it, and it takes them in two distinct ways. Some of what it carries is suspended: particles of clay, fibres, fragments of leaf, small enough to hang in the water and make it cloudy but still, at heart, particles. Given time they settle, and given a filter they can be strained out.

The rest is dissolved. Salt, calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate, sulphate, and traces of nearly everything else in the periodic table have not merely been carried along. They have come apart in the water, separated into charged fragments called ions, each one surrounded by water molecules and barely larger than they are. Dissolved matter does not make water cloudy. Seawater is perfectly clear. It does not settle, however long it is left. And it passes through any ordinary filter as easily as the water itself.

Total dissolved solids is the weight of all of it, per litre. The oldest way to measure it is also the most literal, and it is where the label's wording comes from. Take a known volume of water, filter out the suspended matter, boil the rest away, dry the residue in an oven at 180 degrees so that no water clings to it, and weigh what remains. The standard laboratory method still works exactly this way. The number on the bottle is that weight.

A scale worth carrying around

A measurement only means something in relation to other measurements, and TDS rewards a little memorising. The scale runs over four orders of magnitude, and where a water sits on it tells you most of what you need to know about it.

WaterTDS, mg/L
Rain, freshly fallenaround 10
Typical tap water100 to 500
Brackish groundwater1,000 to 10,000
Seawaterabout 35,000
Brine from a seawater desalination plant60,000 to 80,000

Rain is nearly pure, having been distilled by the sun. By the time it has travelled through a landscape and arrived at a tap it has picked up a few hundred milligrams of minerals per litre, more in limestone country, less on granite. Groundwater that has spent a long time underground can be brackish, too salty to drink but nowhere near the sea. The sea itself, at roughly 35 grams of salt in every litre, is the reference point for everything above it.

The last row is a piece of arithmetic rather than geology, and it matters later. A desalination plant does not remove the salt from seawater so much as move it. If half the water passes through the membranes as fresh water, the other half is left carrying the salt of the whole, and it goes back to the sea roughly twice as concentrated as it arrived.

The taste of nothing

The first thing TDS explains is flavour. Pure water tastes of nothing, and not in a pleasant way. Distilled water, which has a TDS close to zero, is described by most people as flat, slightly odd, and faintly unpleasant, and it is not sold as a drink for that reason. What people experience as the taste of water is the taste of what is dissolved in it: a little calcium and magnesium give it body, bicarbonate gives it a rounded softness, sodium and chloride begin to make it taste salty.

The World Health Organization's drinking water guidelines, which are careful about such things, note that water below about 600 milligrams per litre is generally regarded as good on taste, and that above about 1,000 it becomes increasingly unpalatable to most people. Between those two figures is a matter of preference and habit.

This is also why mineral water brands print the number and advertise the minerals rather than hiding them. The strongest sparkling waters carry well over a thousand milligrams per litre and charge a premium for it. In the same supermarket, a few aisles away, are jugs with cartridges designed to take those same minerals out of tap water. Both products are selling taste. Their customers simply prefer different ones.

Measuring it in a second

No treatment plant boils water in an oven to find out its TDS. Dissolved ions carry an electric charge, and charged particles conduct electricity, so the more of them there are, the more readily a current passes through the water. A TDS meter is a conductivity meter with a conversion factor built into it. Two electrodes on the end of a probe, a small current between them, and a reading on the screen within a second or two.

Every operator carries one, and every operator knows its limits. It is instant, cheap and close enough for most decisions, and it says nothing about which minerals are present, only how much of them there is in total. A water with a TDS of 400 might be hard and harmless or might carry a problem worth knowing about. For that, a sample goes to a laboratory, where each ion is measured on its own. The pen tells you whether to be curious. The lab tells you what to do.

Why dissolved is the hard problem

The second and larger thing TDS explains is the shape of the entire water treatment industry.

Nearly every way of cleaning water works on things that are bigger than water. A sand filter catches particles because they cannot fit between the grains. A settling tank lets heavy things sink. The biological stage of a sewage works uses bacteria to eat organic matter. Even a fine membrane, of the kind that holds back bacteria and viruses, does so because those organisms are far larger than its pores.

Dissolved salt defeats all of them. Its ions are barely bigger than the water molecules around them, so no pore can hold them back while letting water through. They do not sink. Nothing eats them. A conventional treatment plant, the kind that turns sewage into clear water fit to discharge, leaves the TDS almost exactly where it found it. The water goes in salty and comes out clean and salty.

There are only three ways to take salt out of water, and every one of them costs energy.

MethodHow it worksWhere the energy goes
Membrane, reverse osmosisWater is pushed through a membrane at 55 to 80 bar; the salt stays behindHigh pressure pumps
EvaporationThe water is boiled off and condensed; the salt stays behindHeat
Ion exchangeSalt ions are swapped onto a resin, which is later flushed with brineThe salt used to reset the resin, and the brine it produces

Push it through a membrane. Reverse osmosis uses a membrane so tight that water molecules pass and ions, for the most part, do not. Nature pulls in the other direction: when salty water and fresh water sit either side of such a membrane, fresh water flows towards the salt, and for seawater that pull is worth about 27 bar of pressure. To run the process backwards, the plant has to push harder than the sea pulls, so seawater membranes are driven at somewhere between 55 and 80 bar, roughly thirty times the pressure in a car tyre. The pumps that produce that pressure are where the energy goes.

Boil it away. Evaporate the water and the salt stays behind, then condense the vapour. This is how the oldest large desalination plants in the Gulf work, and it is robust and simple, but heating water is one of the most energy hungry things that can be done to it.

Trade it onto a resin. Ion exchange resins are tiny beads that swap the ions in the water for ions they hold on their surface. A household water softener works this way, exchanging the calcium that causes limescale for sodium, which does not. When the beads are full they have to be flushed with strong salt water to reset them, which produces a salty waste of its own. The salt has been moved, again, rather than removed.

The wall at the end of every reuse project

Put those facts together and the central difficulty of the industry comes into view. A factory can treat its wastewater and bring 70 to 90 percent of it back into the process, which is an excellent result. But the salt in that water does not leave with the clean stream. It stays behind in the 10 to 30 percent the membranes rejected, and that stream, called the brine or the concentrate, is now more concentrated than anything the factory started with.

Somebody has to deal with it. Discharged to a river, it moves the problem downstream. Evaporated, it costs heat. Processed to recover the salt for reuse, which is where the most interesting work in the field is happening, it means building something close to a small chemical plant next to the water plant. Every reuse scheme eventually arrives at a meeting about the brine, and the number on the whiteboard in that meeting is TDS.

A caveat on the word high

It is worth being clear about what the measurement does not say. A high TDS says nothing, on its own, about safety. The figure reports how much is dissolved and stays silent about what. Some of the most prized mineral waters in Europe carry more than a thousand milligrams per litre and are drunk with pleasure and without harm. Conversely a water with a modest TDS can carry a specific contaminant that matters. TDS is a measure of taste, of scale and of treatment cost. It is not a measure of danger, and the two are often confused.

Three encounters in a day

The measurement is easier to remember once it is attached to the places it turns up. The scale that forms inside a kettle is calcium and magnesium coming back out of solution when the water is heated; that fraction of TDS has its own name, hardness, and its own article.

The small print on a bottle of mineral water is the same measurement, used as a selling point. The brine leaving a desalination plant on the coast is the same measurement again, now a disposal problem that costs money by the cubic metre.

One number, three settings. It is rarely the headline figure in the water business, and it is the one that decides, more often than any other, what a water can be used for and what it will cost to make it usable.

Sources

  1. World Health Organization, Guidelines for Drinking water Quality, background document on total dissolved solids in drinking water (palatability thresholds).
  2. Directive 2009/54/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council on the exploitation and marketing of natural mineral waters (labelling of dry residue).
  3. APHA, AWWA, WEF. Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewater, method 2540 C (total dissolved solids dried at 180 °C) and 2510 (conductivity).
  4. Photographs: opener: עץ על אי מלח באמצע ים המלח by ערן רזניק (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: TDS Water meter, (2025) by Gpkp (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Solar salt. Grassmere NZ. (8107345297) by Bernard Spragg. NZ from Christchurch, New Zealand (CC0) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Dripping Faucet by Angelsharum (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons.
  5. Salinity ranges and seawater reverse osmosis operating pressures (55 to 80 bar) are standard values from desalination design practice; osmotic pressure of seawater is roughly 27 bar at 35,000 mg/L.

item.title: Thirsty: Paper
item.description:
Every office email footer used to beg the same thing: please consider the environment before printing. That request was worth about 10 litres of water per sheet.
Most of it went through a tree. A plantation pine or eucalyptus drinks rain for years before it becomes pulp, and that patience is what the sheet inherits. The mill's share used to be enormous too, but this is one of industry's quiet success stories. A modern paper mill runs its water in loops and uses about a tenth of what mills used decades ago. The machines improved. The tree still takes its time.
The everyday scale is what makes paper interesting. One sheet is nothing. A ream is 5,000 litres. An office printer that runs through a box of paper a week is quietly moving a swimming pool through it every few months. And the recycled sheet in the same tray skips the tree entirely, which roughly halves the whole number.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
A sheet of office paper carries about 10 litres of water, most of it drunk by a tree over years. The mills that turn the tree into paper have cut their own water tenfold, which makes paper one of industry's quiet successes and the tree the part nobody can shrink.

For a decade or so, most office emails ended with the same small plea in green type: please consider the environment before printing this email. It was easy to mock and easier to ignore, and it never said what, exactly, printing cost. The answer, for water, is about 10 litres per sheet, and where those litres went is a story with a happy middle and a stubborn beginning.

Ten litres

The water footprint of paper was estimated in a 2012 study by Pieter van Oel and Arjen Hoekstra, the first to apply the footprint method to the industry, and the global average for a sheet of printing paper comes out at roughly 10 litres. A sheet of A4 weighs about five grams; a tonne of paper carries something like 2,000 cubic metres of water, most of it in the form of rain that a tree drank.

StageLitresShare
Growing the wood880%
Pulping and milling1.515%
Everything else: bleaching, coating, transport0.55%

The split is approximate; the total is the citable figure. Four fifths of the water in a sheet was used by a plant, which makes paper, in water terms, a crop product like coffee or cotton. The crop simply takes longer.

The tree takes its time

Printing paper is made from wood fibre, and the wood comes mostly from plantation trees grown for the purpose: pine and spruce in the north, eucalyptus in Brazil, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere in the south. A eucalyptus plantation is harvested after around seven years; a northern pine or spruce stand after several decades. For all that time the trees are doing what every plant does, pumping water from the soil into the air through their leaves, and building wood with a small part of it.

The method charges that water to the wood, and through the wood to the paper. A sheet of A4 inherits years of a tree's patience, and there is nothing a mill can do about it, because the tree grew before the mill was involved. This is the part of paper's footprint that nobody can shrink, and it is also, as with most crops, the gentle part. Plantation forestry is overwhelmingly rain fed. Rain on a eucalyptus stand in Portugal was not going to fill a tap.

The plantation itself is a fair subject for argument on other grounds. Eucalyptus is a thirsty tree that has been blamed, in dry regions, for lowering water tables where it replaces native scrub, and a plantation is not a forest. But the water in the sheet, counted the way every footprint here is counted, is mostly green.

The mills cleaned up

The mill's share of the footprint is the part of the story worth telling in an industry article, because it is one of the clearest examples of an industry that fixed its water.

Making paper is a wet process from beginning to end. Wood chips are cooked into pulp with chemicals and water, the pulp is washed and, for white paper, bleached, and it is then spread as a thin slurry, more than 99 percent water, onto a moving wire screen. The water drains and is pressed and dried out of it, and what remains is a sheet. For most of the twentieth century a paper mill used something like 100 cubic metres of water for every tonne of paper it made, and discharged most of it, loaded with fibre, lignin and bleaching chemicals, into the nearest river. The rivers below pulp mills were among the most damaged in the industrial world.

Water used inside a paper mill, per tonne of paper
Mills of the mid twentieth centuryAround 100 cubic metres or more
Good modern millsAround 10 cubic metres
The bestBelow that

Good modern mills use around a tenth of that. The change came from closing the loops: the water that drains through the wire is caught and used again to dilute the next pulp, the washing stages are run in sequence so that the cleanest water does the last wash and the dirtiest the first, the bleaching chemistry moved away from chlorine, and the effluent that does leave is treated in a biological plant before it reaches the river. None of this was exotic. It was engineering, applied over decades under regulatory pressure, and it took an industry that was a byword for river pollution and made it a model of water reuse. The machines improved. The tree still takes its time.

Where the trees grow

The plantation forestry behind paper has moved, over the last half century, from the northern conifer belt to the fast growing south, and the move has a water dimension of its own.

Nordic and Canadian mills still run on spruce and pine from managed forests that regrow over decades, on rain and snowmelt in landscapes with water to spare. The growth of the industry, though, has been in eucalyptus: Brazil above all, where plantations of a few hundred thousand hectares feed some of the largest pulp mills ever built, and Portugal, Spain, Chile, South Africa and Uruguay. Eucalyptus reaches pulping size in about seven years, grows straight, and pulps well, and a hectare of it in a good climate yields several times what a hectare of northern forest does in the same time.

It is also a thirsty tree, and in dry regions that has consequences. Eucalyptus roots deeply and transpires heavily, and where plantations have replaced native scrub or grassland in places with little rain, streams have shrunk and water tables have dropped. South Africa regulates eucalyptus planting for that reason, treating the tree as a stream flow reduction activity that needs a licence. In wet Brazil the same tree is a modest neighbour. As with every crop on this site, the water in the product depends on the address of the plant, and the address of a plantation is a decision somebody made.

Tissue, cardboard and the rest

Printing paper is a small part of what the industry makes, and the water story differs across the range.

Cardboard and packaging, which is now the largest part of the industry's output as printing declines and online shopping grows, is made mostly from recovered fibre, old boxes pulped into new ones, and carries the mill's water without the tree's. It is the paper product that has gone furthest into the loop. Tissue, at the other end, is made mostly from virgin fibre, because recycled fibres are too short to make a soft, strong sheet, and tissue is used once and flushed or binned, so it never returns to the loop at all. Newsprint, which was once the great consumer of recovered fibre, is disappearing with the newspapers. The fibre a society uses moves through this system, from virgin pulp to printing paper to packaging to packaging again, losing length at each turn, and the water in it is highest at the first step and lowest at the last.

The everyday scale

What makes paper worth an article is not the size of its number but the scale at which it is used. One sheet is nothing. A ream of 500 sheets, the box that fits in a printer drawer, is 5,000 litres. A box of five reams is 25,000 litres, the volume of a small swimming pool. An office printer that gets through a box a week is moving a swimming pool of water through it every few months, sheet by sheet, and nobody sees a drop.

Paper, by the unit people actually handleLitres
One sheet of A4about 10
One ream of 500 sheetsabout 5,000
One box of five reamsabout 25,000

The recycled sheet skips the forest

Recycled paper is made from paper, and paper does not grow. A sheet made from recovered fibre skips the tree entirely, and since the tree was four fifths of the footprint, that roughly halves the number: the mill still uses its water, and de inking recovered fibre takes a little more processing than virgin pulp, but the years of rain are not repeated. The printer tray, in this one respect, is a water decision, and it is a decision that costs nothing to make.

The footnote is that fibre cannot be recycled forever.

Europe recovers and reuses a larger share of its paper than any other region, above 70 percent by the industry's own count, and the recovered fibre travels: bales of old cardboard from European and American cities are shipped to mills in Asia, where they become the boxes that carry goods back. The loop is global, and the water in it, as with every product on this site, was spent where the tree grew rather than where the box was folded. Each cycle shortens the fibres, and after five or six rounds they are too short to hold a sheet together, so the system always needs some fresh wood coming in. But a sheet that has been recycled once carried half the water of the one beside it, and most office paper is never recycled at all.

Reading the number

The email footers had a point, and they never said what it was. Ten litres a sheet is small, and five thousand a ream is not, and the difference between them is only the number of sheets. Paper is the product where the mill did its job, decades ago and thoroughly, and where what is left is the slow, gentle, rain fed water of a tree, multiplied by the printer.

Sources

  1. van Oel, P.R. and Hoekstra, A.Y. (2012). Towards quantification of the water footprint of paper: a first estimate of its consumptive component. Water Resources Management 26. Global average on the order of 10 litres per A4 sheet, dominated by the growth of the wood; recycled fibre roughly halves it.
  2. Published pulp and paper mill water benchmarks (CEPI, European Commission BREF for pulp and paper): historical use above 100 m³ per tonne, modern integrated mills around 10 m³ per tonne or below.
  3. South Africa, National Water Act (1998): commercial forestry listed as a stream flow reduction activity requiring a licence.
  4. Stage split (wood, pulping and milling, everything else) is approximate and illustrative; the total is the citable figure.
  5. Photographs: opener: PM-52 Dryer section by Work With Sounds (CC BY-SA) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Old machine used to produce hydrogen paper - Front view by Mervat (CC BY) via Wikimedia Commons; inline: Wood Chips pile ET5A3082 (26916422455) by Intermountain Forest Service, USDA Regio (public domain) via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Food and beverage
item.description:
Cook one dinner and look at the sink afterwards. The colander, the pans, the board covered in potato peel, the water going brown in the bowl. That is a food factory, except it never stops and it handles tonnes an hour.
Food and beverage is a bigger industry than most people picture. Dairies, breweries, bottling plants, bakeries, meat plants, canneries, sugar mills. In Europe it is the largest manufacturing sector there is, and one of the heaviest industrial users of water anywhere.
The strange part is that most of that water never touches the food. Somewhere between half and two thirds of it goes on cleaning the equipment. A crisp factory washes its potatoes, steam peels them, slices them, rinses off the starch, fries, cools, and at the end of the shift washes down the whole line. A dairy pushes hot water and detergent through its own pipework between every batch, and in some plants that cleaning uses more water than the milk it processed.
Nobody can simply wash less. When the product is food, hygiene is not a place to economise. So the industry got clever in another direction: water used in order, cleanest job first, dirtiest last, and the sugary, milky effluent at the end digested into biogas that heats the factory.
The long version, with the tables and the sources, is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water
item.content:encoded:
Europe's largest manufacturing sector is also one of its heaviest industrial users of water, and most of that water never touches the food. It goes on cleaning. How a food factory uses water, why it cannot simply use less, and how the washing up ended up heating the building.

Cook one dinner and look at the sink afterwards. The colander, the pans, the board covered in peel, the water going brown in the bowl. Almost none of that water went into the food. It washed the food, and then it washed everything the food had touched. A food factory is the same sink, except that it never stops, it handles tonnes an hour, and the hygiene rules are written by law.

Food and beverage is a bigger industry than most people picture, and its water is stranger than most people expect. This article is about where it goes.

Bigger than it looks

The industry is made of things that do not seem to belong together: dairies, breweries, bottling plants, bakeries, meat plants, canneries, sugar mills, crisp factories, coffee roasters, juice pressers. Added up, in Europe, they are the largest manufacturing sector there is, larger than cars or chemicals, by turnover and by the number of people employed. They are also, together, one of the heaviest industrial users of water anywhere, because nearly everything they do is wet.

What the water actually does in a food plant
Washes the raw food as it arrivesSoil, leaves, blood, the field
Cleans the machines between batches and shiftsThe largest share
Cools things downCondensers, chillers, cooling tunnels
Raises steamCooking, peeling, sterilising
Becomes part of the productA small share, in drinks and little else
